Rather, you’re maintaining a delicate balance between hundreds of microbial species. At any given time, most of these microorganisms fit into one of two groups: commensals and pathobionts. High quantities of commensals are good for oral health. They minimize inflammation, protect our mouths from harmful foreign microbes, and produce ammonia, which neutralizes tooth-decaying acids. Meanwhile, an abundance of pathobionts is bad for oral health. Sugar-eating varieties produce acid that damages the mouths’ tissues, and meat-eating varieties thrive on the debris inflammation creates. Thorough brushing and flossing remove members of both groups, but commensals can proliferate faster, so they tend to bounce back quicker. This means daily oral hygiene keeps your commensal population higher than your pathobiont population. Most oral disease is the result of this balance being disrupted, and that happens pretty quickly once you stop brushing and flossing. For the first 72 hours, the most notable side effect is supremely bad breath. But by day four, hordes of pathobionts have coated most of your teeth in a sticky film called dental plaque. Over the following days, the plaque triggers an immune response that causes your gums to bleed and inflame— an uncomfortable condition known as gingivitis.
